newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan, Afghan Taleban to start road in January.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan, Afghan Taleban to start road in January.

text.p: Pakistan and Afghanistan are expected to begin construction of a highway in January that will go up to the border of the central Asian republic of Turkmenistan, Pakistani officials said on Thursday.
Pakistan has delivered heavy machinery to Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic movement to build a 100-km (60-mile) portion of the road in the first phase, a senior Foreign Ministry official told Reuters.

Arif Ayub, director general for Afghanistan and South Asia, said this portion, estimated to cost 100 million rupees ($2.5 million), would link Pakistan's southwestern border town of Chaman with the southern Afghan city of Kandahar.

"We have asked the Taleban government that construction of the (Chaman-Kandahar) highway should be completed within six months," he said. "They have assured us that construction would start in the first week of January."
Afghanistan's road network has been destroyed by 17 years of civil war.
Ayub said Pakistan would fund the cost of the highway up to Turkmenistan under an agreement it reached in 1994 with the now ousted Afghan government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani.

After the completion of the first phase, the remaining part of about 400 km (240 miles) of the highway from Kandahar to the Afghan border town of Torghundi will be built and is expected to cost 400 million rupees ($10 million), an official of Pakistan's National Highway Authority said.
With the construction of Chaman-Torghundi highway, Pakistan and Afghanistan will have a road link with Turkmenistan and other Central Asia states, he said.
Torghundi lies on the border of Afghanistan's northwestern province of Badghis and is linked by rail from Turkmenistan.

The road passes through Taleban-held areas except for a small portion in Badghis, which is partly controlled by Taleban and partly by the forces of opposition northern Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Earlier plans to begin road construction in April were not carried out after objections by Rabbani's government, which then controlled the capital Kabul and accused Islamabad of helping the Taleban militia.
The Taleban took Kabul in September, after which Pakistan said it would deal with the radical militia's government as it did with that of Rabbani.
